accuracy.evidence: Every fact in the lab and items was checked against a named source: the cultural iceberg (surface versus deep culture) from Edward T. Hall, Beyond Culture (1976); Hanukkah lasting 8 nights with one more candle each night plus the shamash and Sukkot lasting 7 days (Leviticus 23, Encyclopaedia Britannica); Pongal as a four-day Tamil harvest festival where rice boils over; Chuseok as the Korean harvest festival; Nowruz on the spring equinox; Diwali lamps called diyas; paper and tea from China, Hindu-Arabic numerals from India, maize domesticated in southern Mexico about 9000 years ago, potatoes in the Andes of Peru and Bolivia and Coffea arabica native to Ethiopia (Britannica and Smithsonian entries). Festival cards name one shared reason only where it is the standard description, so none is mis-sorted.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips in teaching cultural diversity: culture as only food, flags and festivals (iceberg prediction 'Yes, that is most of it' and challenge tags food and clothes), ethnocentrism where my way is normal and theirs is weird (Strange to whom prediction, the four two-sides scenes, challenge tags right, wrong and weird), curiosity sliding into stereotype (Stereotype bin, 'Everyone from China eats rice' and the sushi challenge with tags fact and nice), the belief that asking is rude (Curious or unkind prediction) and the Eurocentric belief that our digits came from Europe (Where did it come from prediction).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcult works on culture itself: an iceberg whose waterline splits surface from deep culture, festivals from five faiths and countries matched to a shared reason, a two-sides scene where tapping the other child turns 'weird' into 'tell me more', a three-way curious, put-down or stereotype sort, and a map of where paper, digits, maize, potatoes and coffee began. flaglives (circumstances and judgement), flagalike (same and different, Venn) and flagstereo (counter-examples) share none of these mechanisms; the 30% shingle gate passed against every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds each idea by doing it before any text states it: the iceberg fills with four hidden items under the water and only two or three above, so most of culture is hidden; three festival boxes each collect festivals from different faiths, showing different ways share the same reasons; each scene only resolves when the other child's side is heard; and the origin map fills with five everyday things from five regions, so a normal day is built from many cultures. The done messages then state the rule.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option: 'Yes, that is most of it' for the iceberg, 'Yes, it is how most people do it' for normal habits, 'Yes, best not to ask' for questions about culture, and 'In Europe' for the digits 0 to 9. The task right after each one disproves the wrong pick, and A.reveal quotes the learner's guess in the done message.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with tagged wrong answers, each with its own correction: weird and face (put-downs with or without words), food and clothes (surface culture you can see), same and real (shared idea, not shared story), giveup and nothing (sharing adds, it takes nothing away), fact and nice (a nice-sounding stereotype is still a stereotype), right and wrong (different is not wrong). Sorting and map slips also name the reason, for example 'Not there. Potatoes were first farmed high in the Andes'.

readability.evidence: Kid text reads well inside the learner kid limit of 6.5 with short sentences and named children (Aiko takes her shoes off at home). Adult text stays inside the 9.5 limit while using the precise terms culture, tradition, custom, belief, value, diversity, perspective, stereotype, surface culture, deep culture and ethnocentrism. Card text is one short clause each so it fits two lines at 360 px.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed and overlap with Different Lives and Experiences, Similarities and Differences and Stereotypes stays under the 12% gate. Each kid paragraph carries one idea (iceberg, shared reasons, normal depends on where you grew up, borrowed ideas), and each adult paragraph has one job: curriculum, key terms with the iceberg model, named mistakes, and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark: the iceberg sits on a light sky and sea in both themes so its dark labels stay readable, the festival and talk boxes sit three across about 108 px wide with labels wrapping to two lines, the origin map stacks to a 1-2-2 grid of 160 px tiles, speech bubbles take 90% of the width, and every answer button below the canvas is a full-size tap target.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and iPhone 13, no console or page errors, and all five Show me tasks completed. Every canvas drag or tap has a labelled button twin (Above the water, Festival of lights, Hear Aiko's side, Curious and kind, From India) and the canvas aria-label speaks each result, e.g. 'Aiko: In Japan most homes are shoes-off. Sam now asks to learn more.'
